# School of Math (SOMATH) — full site index

> Complete inventory of every course page, blog post, and guide on schoolofmath.us. Content is organized for LLMs to browse: each link is annotated with a short description drawn from the page's meta description.

For the curated overview, see [llms.txt](https://www.schoolofmath.us/llms.txt).

## Core pages

- [Home](https://www.schoolofmath.us/): NYC math school for grades 1–12. Small groups of 6, Harvard- & Kellogg-trained teachers, free 60-min evaluation. Upper West Side · 226 W 79th St.
- [Math Enrichment Programs NYC](https://www.schoolofmath.us/math-enrichment-nyc): SOMATH's Upper West Side math enrichment programs for grades 1–12. Small in-person classes of 6, teacher-led, on a proprietary 24-class syllabus at every level. Includes a full comparison of enrichment vs. tutoring vs. Kumon vs. math apps.
- [Math Tutor NYC](https://www.schoolofmath.us/math-tutor-nyc): SOMATH's small-group math tutoring in NYC for grades 1–12. Upper West Side classroom, 6-student cap, real teachers, in-person only. Better than a private 1:1 math tutor for most students, at 30–50% of the cost. Compares SOMATH vs. private tutors vs. Kumon vs. Mathnasium vs. RSM vs. apps.
- [About SOMATH](https://www.schoolofmath.us/about): Meet Vivianne Wright (Harvard) and Marcelo Ambrozio (Northwestern) — the educators behind School of Math on the Upper West Side. 20 years preparing GMAT/GRE candidates for top business schools. Now teaching grades 1–12.
- [All courses](https://www.schoolofmath.us/courses): Browse every SOMATH course — Little Newtons, Kid Einsteins, Young Fermats Pre-Algebra, Algebra Ignite, Geometry, Algebra II, SHSAT Prep, SAT Math, and AP Prep. Pick a day and enroll.
- [Contact](https://www.schoolofmath.us/contact): Visit School of Math at 226 West 79th Street, Upper West Side, NYC. Steps from the 1, B, C trains. Open Mon–Fri 3–10pm, Sat 10am–6pm. Call (646) 668-6151.

## SAT Math prep

- [Long Division with Three-Digit Dividends — 25 Practice Questions with Theory & Hidden Answers (Kid Einsteins Class 7, Grades 3–4)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/long-division-3-digit-dividends-kid-einsteins): Class 7 of the SOMATH Kid Einsteins multiplication and division arc — the class where grades 3–4 students move from memorized division facts to long division with dividends up to three digits and one-digit divisors. Covers the DMSB algorithm (Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down) with three fully solved worked examples: 672 ÷ 4 = 168 (no remainder), 754 ÷ 6 = 125 R 4 (with remainder), and 305 ÷ 5 = 61 (zero in the middle of the quotient — write the 0, don't skip). Includes the SOMATH pre-flight checklist (does the divisor fit into the first digit? closest multiplication fact below the chunk? is my subtraction result smaller than the divisor?), the division-check identity dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder used to verify every answer, and how to interpret remainders differently in sharing vs. grouping vs. round-up problems. Then 25 practice questions with click-to-reveal step-by-step solutions grouped by pattern: Q1–Q4 warm-up divisions with no remainder, Q5–Q6 first remainders, Q7 and Q9 zero-in-the-tens-place cases (816 ÷ 8 = 102, 936 ÷ 9 = 104), Q8 and Q10–Q11 and Q13 the group-the-first-two-digits case when the divisor doesn't fit into the leading digit (589 ÷ 7 = 84 R 1, 467 ÷ 5 = 93 R 2, 378 ÷ 6 = 63, 648 ÷ 8 = 81), Q12 zero-in-the-middle with remainder (823 ÷ 4 = 205 R 3), Q14 leading-zero start (500 ÷ 7 = 71 R 3), Q15 the roll-over case (999 ÷ 4 = 249 R 3), Q16 and Q20 clean quotients ending in zero (720 ÷ 6 = 120, 450 ÷ 5 = 90), Q17–Q19 and Q21–Q22 mixed remainders, Q23–Q24 grouped-start cases (504 ÷ 8 = 63, 201 ÷ 7 = 28 R 5), and Q25 the double-zero-in-the-quotient challenge (908 ÷ 9 = 100 R 8). Plus 5 challenge word problems: field-trip buses (round-up remainder), sharing candies (clean divide), pencils in boxes (leftover remainder), weekly savings (fair-share division), and PTA cookies on trays (remainder as leftover). Each problem includes a full DMSB trace and the multiplication check. FAQ covers what to do when the divisor doesn't fit into the first digit, what a subtraction result bigger than the divisor means, how to interpret remainders in word problems, and when two-digit divisors appear (Young Fermats Pre-Algebra, grades 5–6). Includes BlogPosting + FAQPage + LocalBusiness JSON-LD, an answer key table for all 30 questions, and cross-links to Class 6 (Division Facts), Class 5 (Multi-Digit Multiplication), Class 4 (Distributive Thinking & Partial Products), Class 3 (Multiplication Facts ×7 ×8 ×9), the Kid Einsteins course page, and the SOMATH free evaluation. Written by SOMATH — School of Math, 226 W 79th Street, Upper West Side, NYC.
- [Synthetic Division in Calculus — What It Is, Why It Matters, and 5 Practice Questions with Hidden Answers](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/synthetic-division-calculus-5-questions): A pre-calculus and AP Calculus class on synthetic division as a fast shortcut for dividing a polynomial by a linear divisor (x − c). Covers the four-step multiply-and-add algorithm (bring down, multiply by c, add the column, repeat), the Remainder Theorem (remainder equals p(c) with a one-line proof), the Factor Theorem as a corollary, the divide-then-scale trick for non-monic linear divisors (ax + b), and the calculus applications: factoring polynomials with the Rational Root Theorem to find critical points, simplifying 0/0 limits, computing horizontal and slant asymptotes of rational functions, decomposing improper rational functions before partial fractions, and reducing polynomials on AP free-response questions. Then 5 practice questions with click-to-reveal step-by-step answers: (Q1) x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 divided by (x − 1) with full factoring via the Factor Theorem, (Q2) 2x⁴ − 3x² + 5 divided by (x + 1) with missing terms as zero coefficients and p(−1) verified, (Q3) lim (x→2) of (x³ − 7x + 6)/(x − 2) evaluated via synthetic division to 5, (Q4) 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6 fully factored using the Rational Root Theorem plus synthetic division to (x − 3)(2x − 1)(x + 2) with real zeros 3, 1/2, −2, and (Q5) 6x³ + x² − 5x + 2 divided by (2x − 1) using c = 1/2 with quotient coefficients scaled by 1/a to yield 3x² + 2x − 3/2 remainder 1/2, verified two ways. Includes FAQ (fractional quotients, missing terms, AP exam relevance, when to use long division instead), Article + FAQPage + LocalBusiness JSON-LD, and cross-links to SOMATH AP Calculus, AP Pre-Calculus, and Young Fermats Algebra II courses. Written by SOMATH — 226 W 79th St, Upper West Side, NYC.
- [The Top 20 Best Universities in the United States (2026) — Brief Guide to Every School Ranked #1–#20](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/top-20-best-universities-usa-2026): The U.S. News & World Report 2026 Best National Universities ranking distilled to a plain-English brief on every school that landed at rank #1 through #20 — 23 schools total because of ties (four-way tie at #7 among Duke, Johns Hopkins, Northwestern, and Penn; ties at #4, #13, #15, #17, and #20). Covers Princeton #1, MIT #2, Harvard #3, Stanford #4 (tie), Yale #4 (tie), Chicago #6, Duke #7, Johns Hopkins #7, Northwestern #7, Penn #7, Caltech #11, Cornell #12, Brown #13, Dartmouth #13, Columbia #15, UC Berkeley #15, Rice #17, UCLA #17, Vanderbilt #17, Carnegie Mellon #20, Michigan-Ann Arbor #20, Notre Dame #20, and Washington University in St. Louis #20. Each school card lists undergraduate enrollment, acceptance rate, mid-50% SAT range, sticker tuition, financial-aid model, standout programs, and a "best for" summary. Includes a quick-answer ranked table, methodology framing, a 7-item FAQ (What is the #1 school? How many schools are in the top 20 with ties? Which Ivies are in the top 20? Top public universities? How selective are these schools? Is a top-20 school worth the tuition? Where can NYC students prep for the SAT?), Article + FAQPage + LocalBusiness JSON-LD, and cross-links to SOMATH SAT prep resources. Written for NYC high school families by SOMATH — 226 W 79th St, Upper West Side.
- [Multiples & Divisors — 6th Grade Math Class with 25 Practice Questions, Divisibility Rules & Hidden Answers](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/multiples-and-divisors-6th-grade-class): A complete 6th-grade pre-algebra class on multiples and divisors (factors). Covers the vocabulary distinction (multiples go up forever, divisors are a finite list), the pairs method for listing every divisor of a number, the seven divisibility rules (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10) with worked examples, prime vs. composite numbers with the trick number 91 = 7×13, why 1 is neither prime nor composite, prime factorization via factor tree with unique-factorization stated in plain English, GCF and LCM taught both by listing and by prime factorization with the identity GCF×LCM = a×b, and the SOMATH shortcut for word problems (identical groups → GCF, when will cycles line up again → LCM). 25 practice questions plus 5 challenge problems (bake sale bags, blinking lights, largest square tile, divisor-count from prime factorization, smallest number divisible by 1 through 6), each with a click-to-reveal step-by-step answer, plus an answer key table. Written by SOMATH — School of Math, 226 W 79th Street on the Upper West Side, for the Young Fermats Pre-Algebra program (grades 5–6).
- [Barron's Regents Geometry — Practice Exercises 1–11, Fully Solved](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/barrons-regents-geometry-practice-exercises-1-11-walkthrough): All 11 opening practice exercises from Barron's Regents Exams and Answers: Geometry, Sixth Edition. Covers points/lines/planes/coplanar/collinear in a rectangular prism (parallel, perpendicular, skew), the definition of an angle, perpendicular rays with a vertical-angles chase, angle bisector with algebra, parallel lines cut by a transversal with corresponding angles, three-collinear-midpoints with a quadratic equation, zigzag-between-parallels with an auxiliary parallel line, reverse regular-polygon question (156° interior → 15 sides via exterior angles), regular octagon with two sides extended to an exterior point (quadrilateral sum with reflex angle at the concave vertex), regular hexagon diagonals meeting at the center, and the two-column proof that vertical angles are congruent. Each question has a click-to-reveal answer plus a theory recap. Written by SOMATH — School of Math, 226 W 79th Street on the Upper West Side.

## AP Calculus

- [Math Enrichment vs Math Tutoring: A Clear Explanation for NYC Parents](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/math-enrichment-vs-tutoring-nyc): Pillar/definitional guide for NYC families deciding between math enrichment and math tutoring. Opens with the one-line answer: math tutoring is reactive (it fixes a specific school problem by following the school's syllabus toward a concrete outcome like a bad quiz grade, a coming unit test, a Regents/AP exam, or an SHSAT/SAT date) while math enrichment is proactive (it teaches problem-solving strategies, competition thinking, and material one to three years above grade level on its own year-round schedule, regardless of what the school is covering). Tutoring closes gaps; enrichment raises ceilings. Includes single-paragraph definitions of each service, a full side-by-side comparison table across purpose / time horizon / curriculum / success signal / group size / when to start / typical duration / homework style / best-for student profile / NYC price range, a three-question decision tree that routes families to tutoring (any acute school problem), enrichment (bored or coasting student), or enrichment as long-term investment (solid-B student before middle/high-school stakes rise), what a real enrichment class looks like (custom curriculum vs. school textbook, small same-level groups, fewer harder problems, competition exposure via AMC/MATHCOUNTS/Math Kangaroo/SHSAT/Hunter, visible ladder), what real tutoring looks like (written goal, school-syllabus alignment, tutor watching the child do their own homework, sessions that taper off, test-specific prep for SHSAT/SAT/ACT/Regents/AP), the four cases when a child should do both simultaneously (bright child in a hard school, exam year with an existing gap, post-move/gap-year student, two-track family), how SOMATH combines both from one classroom (free evaluation with cofounder Marcelo Ambrozio, honest recommendation of enrichment/tutoring/both, small-group placement into the 24-class ladder, targeted tutoring layered on when needed, monthly parent notes), plus a 6-item FAQ (is enrichment just Kumon?, what age to start on UWS, NYC price ranges, how to tell if a program is working, does SOMATH also do SHSAT/Hunter/SAT/AP prep, how SOMATH differs from RSM/Mathnasium/Kumon). Written for SOMATH — School of Math, 226 W 79th St, Upper West Side, New York.
- [The Four Operations — Mixed Review with Theory (Grades 3–4): 4-Digit Addition with Carrying, 4-Digit Subtraction with Borrowing, 3-Digit Multiplication & Basic Division](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/four-operations-mixed-review-grade-3-4): A grade 3–4 mixed-review pack covering all four operations in one lesson. Full theory on the standard addition algorithm with carrying (regrouping when a column sum is 10 or more, place-value re-packing, why the little carry-1 above the next column is actually one whole ten/hundred/thousand), the standard subtraction algorithm with borrowing/regrouping (including the double-borrow case when you have to travel through zeros — 5,203 − 2,847 style — and how each middle zero becomes a 9), 3-digit × 1-digit multiplication with the standard algorithm (carry gets ADDED to the next partial product, not multiplied), 3-digit × 2-digit multiplication with two partial products and the shift-left rule (writing the 0 in the ones column of the second partial product because you're really multiplying by the tens digit × 10), and division as the inverse of multiplication (fact families, quotient/dividend/divisor vocabulary, special cases: n÷1, n÷n, 0÷n, and why n÷0 is undefined, plus the check-by-multiplication habit). 20 practice questions with click-to-reveal step-by-step answers and the exact standard-algorithm work: 5 addition problems (4,527+3,168; 6,478+2,395; 5,689+4,357; 3,896+5,749; 7,948+1,675) with 4-digit carrying including one that crosses into the ten-thousands, 5 subtraction problems (5,203−2,847; 6,412−3,789; 7,000−2,485; 8,315−4,687; 9,102−5,468) with 4-digit borrowing including the famous 7,000-minus-something all-zeros case and a compensation trick, 5 multiplication problems (234×6; 417×8; 356×7; 625×9; 216×34) with 3-digit numbers ending in a 3-digit × 2-digit problem, and 5 basic division facts (24÷6; 35÷5; 42÷7; 63÷9; 81÷9) taught as multiplication questions with fact families and the ×9 digit-sum trick. Includes a fully worked Regents Part I Q8: 'In △ABC, CE line is the perpendicular bisector of AEB. Which statement is always true?' — answer (1) AC ≅ BC by the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem, with full distractor diagnosis for (2) AE ≅ CE (mixing half-base with apex-to-midpoint segment), (3) ∠EAC ≅ ∠BCE (wrong angle pair — the base angles ∠EAC ≅ ∠EBC and apex-bisected pair ∠ACE ≅ ∠BCE are correct), and (4) m∠A + m∠B = 90° (only true for a right angle at C). Covers rigid-motion sequences (Q25 — reflection over the y-axis then translate 1 left/8 down maps DAN to MIK), parallelogram alternate-interior angles and linear pairs (Q26 — angle CSA = 111°), cylinder volume and density (Q27 — 353 lb), converse of the side-splitter theorem (Q28 — FD = 48), the SAS trig area formula ½ab·sin(C) (Q29 — 32.7 sq units), the angle-bisector construction with compass and straightedge (Q30), and the diagonals-congruent rectangle test (Q31 — RM = 2·RP = 24 = GA, so GRAM is a rectangle). Includes rubric notes for full 2-credit answers. Prepared by SOMATH — School of Math, an Upper West Side math school.
- [Regents Geometry June 2026 — Part III Answers & Explanations (Questions 32–34)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/regents-geometry-june-2026-part-3-answers): Every 4-credit Part III medium-length question from the June 2026 NYS Geometry Regents, worked step-by-step with the theorem and rubric behind each one. Q32 combines angle of elevation (36°) and angle of depression (18°) from one observer to find a building's height across an 80-ft gap, TB = 80·tan(36°) + 80·tan(18°) ≈ 84 ft. Q33 uses the pyramid volume formula V = (1/3)·s²·h with density 1.25 g/cm³ to determine the maximum number of solid clay pyramids from 15 kg of clay — 15,000 g ÷ 480 g per pyramid = 31.25 → 31 pyramids (floor). Q34 is a two-column similar-triangles proof: given AB ≅ AC and DE, HF perpendicular to BC, prove DE/BE = HF/CF using the isosceles-triangle base-angle theorem and AA similarity. Prepared by SOMATH — School of Math, an Upper West Side math school.
- [Regents Geometry June 2026 — Part IV Answer & Full 6-Credit Solution (Question 35)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/regents-geometry-june-2026-part-4-answers): Every step of the 6-credit Part IV coordinate-geometry question on the June 2026 NYS Geometry Regents, worked with the theorem behind each move. Triangle ABC has A(-3,-1), B(-5,2), C(-1,8). Part (a): use the fact that diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other to find D(1, 5). Part (b): prove ABCD is a parallelogram by showing both pairs of opposite sides have equal slopes — slope AB = slope DC = -3/2, slope BC = slope AD = 3/2. Part (c): midpoint formula gives E = midpoint(BC) = (-3, 5). Part (d): distance formula shows AB = BE = √13, so △ABE is isosceles by definition. Includes rubric notes for full 6-credit responses. Prepared by SOMATH — School of Math, an Upper West Side math school.

## Analytic geometry & functions

- [Analytic Geometry Q3 (Stewart 9e): Circle Center & Radius](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/analytic-geometry-circle-stewart-calculus): Stewart Calculus 9th Edition diagnostic test, analytic geometry Problem 3 — find the center and radius of the circle x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 10y + 9 = 0. Complete the square step by step, rewrite in standard form, and read off center (3, -5) and radius 5. Worked from SOMATH on the Upper West Side.
- [Analytic Geometry Q1 (Stewart 9e): Equation of a Line](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/analytic-geometry-diagnostic-stewart-calculus): Stewart Calculus 9th Edition diagnostic test, analytic geometry Problem 1 — find the equation of a line through (2, -5) under four conditions: slope -3, parallel to the x-axis, parallel to the y-axis, parallel to 2x - 4y = 3. Worked step by step from SOMATH on the Upper West Side.
- [Equation of a Circle from Center & Point (Stewart 9e Q2)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/circle-equation-from-center-and-point-stewart-calculus): Stewart Calculus 9th Edition diagnostic test, analytic geometry Problem 2 — find the equation of the circle with center (-1, 4) that passes through (3, -2). Standard form, distance-formula shortcut, and the final answer (x+1)^2 + (y-4)^2 = 52. Worked from SOMATH on the Upper West Side.
- [Coordinate Geometry: Line, Midpoint & Circle (Ch.1 Q4)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/coordinate-geometry-points-line-circle-stewart-q4): Stewart Calculus 9th Edition diagnostic Q4 — given A(-7, 4) and B(5, -12), find the slope, line equation, intercepts, midpoint, distance, perpendicular bisector, and the equation of the circle with AB as a diameter. Answer (x+1)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 100. Worked from SOMATH on the Upper West Side.
- [Difference Quotient of f(x) = x³ at x = 2 (Ch.1 Q2)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/difference-quotient-x-cubed-stewart-ch1-q2): Stewart Calculus Chapter 1, Question 2 — evaluate the difference quotient [f(2+h) − f(2)] / h for f(x) = x³ and simplify. Answer: h² + 6h + 12. Step-by-step walkthrough with the binomial expansion of (2+h)³, the algebra of cancelling h, and the link to f′(2) = 12. From SOMATH on the Upper West Side.
- [Reading a Function from Its Graph (Stewart Ch.1 Q1)](https://www.schoolofmath.us/posts/reading-function-graph-domain-range-stewart-ch1-q1): Stewart Calculus Chapter 1, Question 1 — read function values, solve f(x) = 2, estimate zeros, and state the domain and range from a graph. f(-1) = -2, f(2) ≈ 2.8, x = -3 and 1 for f(x) = 2, zeros near -2.3 and 0.3, domain [-3, 3], range [-2, 3].
